title: Chebyshev Lower Bound: Real-Valued π(2n) ≥ (n·log 4 − log(2n+1)) / log(2n)
description: Derives the explicit real-valued lower bound on π(2n) from the Chebyshev integer inequality 4ⁿ ≤ (2n+1)·C(2n,n) ≤ (2n+1)·(2n)^{π(2n)}, completing the analytical bridge to the Prime Number Theorem.

overview.historicalContext:
Pafnuty Chebyshev (1821–1894), working in St. Petersburg, was the first mathematician to prove **explicit** bounds on $\pi(x)$, the count of primes up to $x$. In his 1852 paper *Mémoire sur les nombres premiers*, he established that the ratio $\pi(x)\log(x)/x$ is always between 0.921 and 1.106 — roughly, primes occur neither too densely nor too sparsely. His method was elementary yet powerful: he exploited properties of the central binomial coefficient $C(2n,n)$ and the Chebyshev $\psi$-function (the log-weighted prime sum) to derive double-sided bounds without complex analysis.

Half a century later, Hadamard and de la Vallée Poussin (independently, 1896) proved the **Prime Number Theorem**: $\pi(x) \sim x/\log x$, i.e., the ratio approaches 1. Their proofs required the Riemann zeta function and complex analysis. Chebyshev's elementary technique could not achieve ratio 1, but it established the correct order of magnitude — a feat that stood for 44 years.

This Lean proof file is the analytical capstone of a chain: ChebyshevBounds.lean (integer inequalities on $C(2n,n)$) → ChebyshevPNTBridge.lean (power bounds on $\pi(2n)$) → here (real-valued lower bound). The weaker constants $\log 2 \approx 0.693$ and $2\log 4 \approx 2.773$ (vs. Chebyshev's original 0.921 and 1.106) reflect the use of the simpler $4^n \leq (2n+1)C(2n,n)$ bound in place of Chebyshev's more refined multi-term product construction.
overview.problemStatement:
**Open Question from ChebyshevPNTBridge.lean**:

The integer inequality $4^n \leq (2n+1) \cdot (2n)^{\pi(2n)}$ was proved in the main bridge file. But what explicit real-valued lower bound on $\pi(2n)$ does this give? The answer requires taking logarithms and dividing by $\log(2n)$.
overview.text: For all n ≥ 1: $(n \cdot \log 4 - \log(2n+1)) / \log(2n) \leq \pi(2n)$. Combined with the known upper bound, this gives the full Chebyshev interval for π(2n).
overview.proofStrategy:
**Three-step chain**:
1. $n \cdot \log 4 - \log(2n+1) \leq \log C(2n,n)$ [ChebyshevBounds.log_centralBinom_ge]
2. $\log C(2n,n) \leq \pi(2n) \cdot \log(2n)$ [ChebyshevPNTBridge.centralBinom_le_pow_primeCounting + Real.log_pow]
3. Divide by $\log(2n) > 0$ [Real.log_pos, since $2n \geq 2 > 1$]

The positivity lemma ($4^n > 2n+1$) is proved by induction: base $n=1$ gives $4 > 3$; inductive step uses $2(k+1)+1 = 2k+3 < 4(2k+1) \leq 4 \cdot 4^k = 4^{k+1}$.
keyInsights: The lower bound chains two sandwich inequalities via log: 4^n ≤ (2n+1)·C(2n,n) ≤ (2n+1)·(2n)^π(2n).
Taking log and rearranging gives n·log4 - log(2n+1) ≤ π(2n)·log(2n), then dividing by log(2n) > 0.
The bound is always non-vacuous: 4^n > 2n+1 for all n ≥ 1, proved by elementary induction.
For large n, the lower bound grows as n·log(4)/log(2n) ~ log(2)·(n/log n), confirming π(x) ≳ log(2)·(x/log x).
The upper bound (from Erdos31PrimesDensity) and this lower bound together give the complete Chebyshev interval log(2) ≤ π(2n)·log(2n)/n ≤ 2·log(4) + o(1).
prerequisites: Real.log monotonicity and the log_pow identity

sections.title: Lower Bound (Log Form)
sections.summary: chebyshev_lower_log: n·log4 − log(2n+1) ≤ π(2n)·log(2n). Chains log_centralBinom_ge with centralBinom_le_pow_primeCounting via Real.log_le_log, then applies Real.log_pow.
sections.mathContext: The key identity: log((2n)^{π(2n)}) = π(2n)·log(2n) by Real.log_pow. Combined with log(C(2n,n)) ≤ log((2n)^{π(2n)}) from C(2n,n) ≤ (2n)^{π(2n)}.

sections.title: Lower Bound (Divided Form)
sections.summary: chebyshev_lower_real: (n·log4 − log(2n+1)) / log(2n) ≤ π(2n). Divides the log form by log(2n) > 0 using div_le_iff₀.
sections.mathContext: log(2n) > 0 since 2n ≥ 2 > 1 for n ≥ 1. The division is valid and the bound is non-trivial.

sections.title: Positivity of the Lower Bound
sections.summary: chebyshev_lower_pos: 0 < n·log4 − log(2n+1). Proved via 4^n > 2n+1 by induction.

sections.title: Upper Bound (Re-export)
sections.summary: chebyshev_upper_real: π(N) ≤ 2·N·log4/logN + √N + 1. Direct re-export from Erdos31PrimesDensity.
sections.mathContext: The upper bound was proved independently in Erdos31PrimesDensity as part of showing primes have density zero.

sections.title: Combined Chebyshev Interval
sections.summary: chebyshev_pi_interval: π(2n) is sandwiched between the lower and upper Chebyshev bounds for n ≥ 2.
sections.mathContext: Combines chebyshev_lower_real (new) and chebyshev_upper_real (re-export) into a single interval statement.

sections.title: Numerical Verifications
sections.summary: native_decide verifications: π(2)=1, π(10)=4, π(20)=8, π(100)=25, π(1000)=168.

crossReferences.description: ChebyshevPNTBridge.lean proved the integer power bounds. This file converts them to real-valued bounds via logarithms.
OQ01 proved the Kummer-theorem-based version of the central binomial bound. Both approaches give the same final integer inequality.

conclusion.summary: The explicit real-valued Chebyshev lower bound π(2n) ≥ (n·log4 − log(2n+1))/log(2n) is proved, completing the analytical bridge from integer power inequalities to explicit bounds on the prime counting function. Four theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical significance**: This closes the main open question from ChebyshevPNTBridge.lean: what explicit real bound does the integer inequality give? The answer is the Chebyshev lower bound, which confirms π(x) ≳ log(2)·(x/log x) with an explicit constant.

**Combined with the upper bound**: The full Chebyshev interval [log(2)−ε, 2·log(4)+ε] for the ratio π(2n)·log(2n)/n is now completely formalized. This represents Chebyshev's 1852 result with weaker constants (0.693 vs 0.921 lower, 2.773 vs 1.106 upper).
openQuestions: Can the lower constant be tightened from log(2) ≈ 0.693 to Chebyshev's original 0.921 using a more refined analysis of C(2n,n)?
Can the upper constant be tightened from 2·log(4) ≈ 2.773 to 1.106 using a finer sieve?
